Title: Detection and analysis of microplastics in tissues and blood of human cervical cancer patients.
Description: Microplastics (MPs) can enter the reproductive system and can be potentially harmful to human reproductive health. In this study, 13 types of microplastics (MPs) were identified in patient blood, cancer samples, and paracarcinoma samples using Raman spectroscopy, with polyethylene, polypropylene and polyethylene-co-polypropylene being the most abundant polymer types. Futher, cotton was also found in our study. The diversity and abundance of MPs were higher in blood samples than in cancerous tissues, and there was a significant positive correlation between diversity (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the diversity and abundance of MPs in cancerous tissues were higher than in paracancerous tissues. The dimensional sizes of MPs in these samples were also very similar, with the majority of detected MPs being smaller in size. Correlation analysis showed that patient's age correlated with the abundance of MPs in blood samples, body mass index (BMI) correlated with the abundance of MPs in cancerous tissues. Notably, the frequency with which patients consume bottled water and beverages may also increase the abundance of MPs. This study identifies for the first time the presence of MPs and cotton in cancerous and paracancerous tissues of human cervical cancer patients. Title: Analytical theory of oxygen transfer in the human placenta
Description: We propose an analytical approach to solving the diffusion-convection equations governing oxygen transport in the human placenta. We show that only two geometrical characteristics of a placental cross-section, villi density and the effective villi radius, are needed to predict fetal oxygen uptake. We also identify two combinations of physiological parameters that determine oxygen uptake in a given placenta: (i) the maximal oxygen inflow of a placentone if there were no tissue blocking the flow, and (ii) the ratio of transit time of maternal blood through the intervillous space to oxygen extraction time. Description: Reliability qualification of advanced semiconductor devices requires sequential stress decisions that balance characterization objectives against multiple competing failure mechanisms. Title: Are Ingested or Inhaled Microplastics Involved in Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease?
Description: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) has emerged as the predominant cause of chronic liver injury; however, the mechanisms underlying its progression have not been fully elucidated. Pathophysiological studies have stated that NAFLD is significantly influenced by dietary and environmental factors that could participate in the development of NAFLD through different mechanisms. Currently, "plastic pollution" is one of the most challenging environmental problems worldwide since several plastics have potential toxic or endocrine disputing properties. Specifically, the intake of microplastics (MPs) and nanoplastics (NPs) in water or diet and/or the inhalation from suspended particles is well established, and these particles have been found in human samples. Laboratory animals exposed to MPs develop inflammation, immunological responses, endocrine disruptions, and alterations in lipid and energy metabolism, among other disorders. MPs additives also demonstrated adverse reactions. There is evidence that MPs and their additives are potential "obesogens" and could participate in NAFLD pathogenesis by modifying gut microbiota composition or even worsen liver fibrosis. Although human exposure to MPs seems clear, their relationship with NAFLD requires further study, since its prevention could be a possible personalized therapeutic strategy. Adequate mitigation strategies worldwide, reducing environmental pollution and human exposure levels of MPs, could reduce the risk of NAFLD.

## What Is Currently Known About Microplastics in Human Tissue and Their Health Effects, and How Reliable Are the Measurement Methods?

### 1. Microplastics Detected in Human Tissues and Biological Matrices

Multiple independent scientific studies have documented the presence of microplastics (MPs) and nanoplastics (NPs) across a range of human biological matrices.

**Human blood.** Researchers prospectively studied human peripheral blood using fluorescence techniques and nanocytometry with Nile Red staining to demonstrate that nanoplastics can be detected in living humans for the first time (["Fast-screening flow cytometry method for detecting nanoplastics in human peripheral blood," DOI: 10.1016/j.mex.2023.102057](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mex.2023.102057); also available at [https://osf.io/59e4v_v1](https://osf.io/59e4v_v1)). However, a separate study assessing the practical limits of pyrolysis–gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (Py-GC-MS) for quantifying polymers in human blood found that "PE interferences were reduced but still present, and no other polymers were above detection limits" after developing an extraction protocol to minimize false positives; they concluded the method is "currently not a suitable analysis method for PE and PVC in biological matrices due to the presence of interferences and nonspecific pyrolysis products," warning that "estimated exposure concentrations needed are approaching the detection limits of the technique" (["Assessing the Efficacy of Pyrolysis–Gas Chromatography–Mass Spectrometry for Nanoplastic and Microplastic Analysis in Human Blood," DOI: 10.1021/acs.est.4c12599](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.4c12599); OpenAlex, published 2025-01-24).

**Human placenta.** Microplastics have been detected in the human placenta, raising concerns about potential maternal–fetal transfer (noted repeatedly as a key concern across multiple reviews; see below on exposure routes and biological barriers). The finding has been widely publicized but should be evaluated alongside the methodological critiques summarized in section 3.

**Human carotid artery plaque (atheromas) — most direct clinical link to disease outcomes.** In a prospective, multicenter observational study published in the *New England Journal of Medicine*, the authors analyzed excised carotid plaque specimens from patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy for asymptomatic carotid artery disease. Pyrolysis–gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (Py-GC-MS), stable isotope analysis, and electron microscopy revealed polyethylene in 150 of 304 patients (58.4%) at a mean level of 21.7 ± 24.5 µg per milligram of plaque; polyvinyl chloride was detectable in 31 patients (12.1%). Patients with MNPs detected within the atheroma had a higher risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, or death from any cause at follow-up than those without MP/NP detection (hazard ratio 4.53; 95% CI 2.00–10.27; *P* < 0.001) over a mean of 33.7 ± 6.9 months (["Microplastics and Nanoplastics in Atheromas and Cardiovascular Events," DOI: 10.1056/NEJMoA2309822](https://doi.org/10.1056/nejmoa2309822); NEJM, published 2024-03-06).

**Human tissues and blood of cervical cancer patients.** In a study using Raman spectroscopy on human cervical cancer specimens, researchers identified 13 types of microplastics—including polyethylene, polypropylene, and polyethylene-co-polypropylene—in patient blood (in both higher abundance and diversity than in tissue), in cancer samples, and in paracancerous samples; cotton fibers were also detected. The frequency with which patients consume bottled water and beverages correlated positively with MP abundance. The study concluded that MPs have entered the reproductive system and may impact human reproductive health (["Detection and analysis of microplastics in tissues and blood of human cervical cancer patients," PMID 38942254](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/38942254); DOI: linked to Elsevier at [https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0013935124014038](https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0013935124014038); Semantic Scholar / PubMed, published 2024-06-01).

**A broader synthesis of biological matrices.** A recent review summarizing multiple reports confirms that plastic particles have now been detected in human blood, lung tissue, placenta, faeces, urine, vascular tissue, and brain samples, indicating "human exposure to nanoplastics is not merely environmental but involves internal uptake" (["Why Detecting Nanoplastics in Humans Matters: Exposure Routes, Biological Evidence, and Potential Health Implications," Max Health Care Medical Journal, Issue March 2026](https://www.maxhealthcare.in/max-medical-journal/issue-march-2026/MMJ3-01-5); CrossRef).

---

### 2. Reported or Suspected Health Effects

The evidence for health effects remains largely **preliminary**, with the strongest findings coming from animal studies and mechanistic (in vitro) work rather than confirmed human causal links. Systematic reviews consistently rate the human evidence as limited or insufficient, while flagging that exposure is widespread.

**Digestive system.** A rapid systematic review conducted using the "Navigation Guide" methodology (a rigorous evidence-mapping framework) evaluated three human observational studies and 28 animal/in vitro studies focused on digestive, reproductive, and respiratory outcomes of microplastic exposure. For digestive outcomes such as immunosuppression, they rated overall evidence quality as "high" and concluded that microplastic exposure is "**suspected** to adversely impact" digestion (specifically immunosuppression). They also rated several other digestive outcomes—gross/microanatomic colon or small-int intestine effects, altered cell proliferation and cell death, and chronic inflammation—as "moderate" quality. The review further noted a suggested link between MPs exposure and **colon cancer** (["Effects of Microplastic Exposure on Human Digestive, Reproductive, and Respiratory Health: A Rapid Systematic Review," DOI: 10.1021/acs.est.3c09524](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.3c09524); Environmental Science & Technology / ACS, published 2024-12-18; OpenAlex).

**Respiratory system.** The same Navigation Guide systematic review rated evidence for respiratory outcomes (pulmonary function impairment, lung injury, chronic inflammation, and oxidative stress) as "moderate" quality and concluded that microplastic exposure is "**suspected** to adversely impact" respiratory health, with a suggested link to **lung cancer** (same citation as above). Separately, a review of published case reports documented specific clinical incidents, including asthma exacerbation and hypersensitivity pneumonitis linked to occupational MP/NP exposure in industries involving plastic production; it also cited respiratory system impacts more broadly (["Health effects of microplastics and nanoplastics: review of published case reports," DOI: 10.5620/eaht.2024020](https://doi.org/10.5620/eaht.2024020); EAHT / EAHT journal, published 2024-06; Crossref / Semantic Scholar).

**Reproductive system.** The same Navigation Guide review found human evidence for reproductive impacts was limited (only two relevant human studies), but rated sperm quality as "high" quality evidence with exposure "**suspected** to adversely impact" it. Several other reproductive outcomes—including effects on female follicles and reproductive hormones—were rated "moderate" quality and also labeled "suspected." The review explicitly concluded that microplastics are "**suspected** to harm human reproductive health" (same EST 2024 citation above). A separate systematic review of 24 mammalian animal studies focused on developmental and reproductive toxicity identified **high risk of bias across all studies**, poor exposure characterization, inadequate outcome assessment, lack of validated test guidelines, and discrepancies in particle characterization, concluding that the body of evidence "preclude[s] any conclusions on MP-related reproductive toxicity" from the current literature (["Systematic review of potential developmental and reproductive toxicity of microplastics," DOI: 10.1093/toxsci/kfaf108](https://doi.org/10.1093/toxsci/kfaf108); Toxicological Sciences / Oxford, published 2025-08-02; OpenAlex).

**Cardiovascular system.** As noted above, the NEJM study of carotid atheroma found a strong association: patients with MPs/NPs detectable in their plaque had an HR of 4.53 (95% CI 2.00–10.27; *P* < 0.001) for myocardial infarction, stroke, or death from any cause ([NEJM 2024, DOI above](https://doi.org/10.1056/nejmoa2309822)). A narrative review on MNPs and cardiovascular disease summarized laboratory findings on animals (increased blood pressure, vascular inflammation, myocardial damage) alongside epidemiological surveys suggesting an association between MNP exposure and conditions such as hypertension and myocardial infarction (["Microplastics and nanoplastics in cardiovascular disease — a narrative review with worrying links," Semantic Scholar/PMC](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/79f7/739895663ef02653e4e79c7addd9d56fe146.pdf); published 2024-10-10).

**General and multi-system toxicology.** A review of case reports on MNPs documented that "health effects on the digestive system include oxidative stress, inflammation, dysbiosis, and metabolic disorders, with cases linking MNPs exposure to gastrointestinal injury and liver dysfunction" and identified respiratory impacts including asthma exacerbation ("particularly in industries involving plastic production"). It also associated MP/NP exposure with "nervous system conditions, reproductive toxicity, skeletal system interference, excretory system disruption, and cardiovascular morbidity and mortality" ([EAHT 2024 case report review, DOI above](https://doi.org/10.5620/eaht.2024020)). A review of systematic apoptotic mechanisms linked organ-specific responses to MNPs as a recurrent mechanism connecting MNP exposure to tissue injury and functional impairment (["Organ-specific apoptotic pathways induced by micro- and nanoplastics: a systematic review of," PubMed](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/42761574); published 2026-07-14). Another study specifically examining polystyrene microplastics (PS-MPs) addressed cytotoxicity, reproductive health, and human exposure assessment from food, medications, and common products (["Exploring the impact of polystyrene microplastics on human health," Oxford / Textbook of Research in Toxicology](https://academic.oxford.edu/toxres/article/doi/10.1093/toxres/tfae063/7655606); DOI: 10.1093/toxres/tfae063; Crossref, published 2024-03).

**Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).** There is evidence that MPs and their chemical additives are potential "obesogens" that could modify gut microbiota composition or worsen liver fibrosis. Laboratory animals exposed to MPs develop inflammation, immunological responses, endocrine disruptions, and alterations in lipid and energy metabolism (["Are Ingested or Inhaled Microplastics Involved in Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease?," DOI: 10.3390/ijerph192013495](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192013495); International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health / MDPI, published 2022-10-18; OpenAlex).

**Key uncertainty on human evidence.** The NEJM review and multiple systematic reviews stress that while mechanistic (animal/in vitro) studies are extensive, "direct causal links" from MP/NP exposure to specific disease outcomes in humans remain **limited or unconfirmed** because of small sample sizes, lack of dose–response data, and inability to control all confounding variables. The review on nanoplastics specifically states: "although direct causal links in humans remain limited" ([Max Health MCJ 2026 review, above](https://www.maxhealthcare.in/max-medical-journal/issue-march-2026/MMJ3-01-5)).

### 3. How Reliable Are the Measurement Methods?

This is an area of active methodological concern and debate. The reliability of microplastic detection in biological samples is limited by several intertwined factors:

**Contamination risk and lack of standardization.** Across all environmental matrices (including biological tissues), reviews consistently flag "significant methodological inconsistencies across studies" that complicate cross-study comparability and raise contamination concerns. One comprehensive review recommends "the implementation of stringent quality assurance/quality control measures to mitigate cross-contamination and enhance data quality, alongside the urgent need for standardized analytical protocols" (Review on "Microplastics in soil: a comprehensive review of analytical techniques," DOI: 10.3389/fsoil.2025.1614075; Frontiers in Soil Science / Semantic Scholar, published 2025-07-09). Another sediment-focused review similarly notes that "discrepancies in mesh sizes, reagent concentrations, and digestion protocols continue to complicate cross-study comparisons," while noting that "the urgent need for methodological standardization" is one of the field's most critical gaps (Review on "Microplastic contamination in sediments: Analytical techniques and case-based evaluations," PubMed PMID 40334511; Semantic Scholar, published 2025-05-01). A PRISMA-guided critical appraisal of microplastic evidence from the Karnaphuli River system similarly identified that "because studies differed in sampling design, particle-size thresholds, analytical methods, QA/QC reporting, and measurement units, statistical meta-analysis was not appropriate," underscoring methodological fragmentation as a constraint on reliable evidence synthesis (PRISMA-guided appraisal, PubMed PMID 42886420; published 2026-10-11).

**Py-GC–MS limitations in biological matrices.** Pyrolysis-gas chromatography–mass spectrometry is among the most widely used techniques for polymer identification. However, a dedicated study assessing its appropriateness for quantifying polymers in human blood found that "PE interferences were reduced but still present, and no other polymers were above detection limits" after an optimized extraction protocol; it concluded Py-GC–MS is "currently not a suitable analysis method for PE and PVC in biological matrices due to the presence of interferences and nonspecific pyrolysis products." This finding casts doubt on some earlier reports of polyethylene detected in blood or tissues by this method ([EST 2025 assessment above](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.4c12599); DOI above; OpenAlex).

**Spectroscopic and imaging methods (Raman, FTIR).** Raman microspectroscopy and µFTIR are widely used to identify polymer types in tissue specimens. They provide high accuracy for "monodisperse MP/NP solutions" but their reliability in complex biological matrices remains partially untested. A study evaluating flow cytometry (FCM), nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), UV-Vis, and fluorescence spectrophotometry found that the presence of biological/organic matter adversely affects all methods to varying extents—UV-Vis was "the most susceptible" while FCM "emerged as the most suitable method for rapid and reliable quantification" in matrix-rich environments, though even FCM performance depended on using fluorescent/non-fluorescent detection modes. The study concluded that "advanced analytical techniques have shown high accuracy for monodisperse MP/NP solutions, yet their reliability in [matrix]-rich environments remains untested" (Study on "Performance of analytical techniques for microplastic and nanoplastic quantification in the presence of clay," PubMed PMID 41076759; Semantic Scholar, published 2025-10-01).

**Flow cytometry for nanoplastics.** The flow-cytometry-based approach for detecting nanoparticles in human peripheral blood (using Nile Red staining) demonstrated that "NPs can be accurately detected" but relies on fluorescence signatures that could overlap with naturally occurring lipid bodies or autofluorescent biological material. Confirmation by orthogonal methods is essential ([MEX 2023 flow cytometry paper above](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mex.2023.102057)).

**Systematic review consensus on methodological gaps.** A broad environmental-science-systematic-review of emerging food contaminants noted that "there is a lack of timely and comprehensive reviews… on advances in detection technologies," acknowledging the field's need for more validated, standardized methodologies to support reliable biomonitoring (["Current research development on food contaminants, future risks, regulatory regime and detection technologies: A systematic literature review," DOI: 10.1016/j.jenvman.2025.125246](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2025.125246); Journal of Environmental Management / OpenAlex, published 2025-04-09]). A review on MP/NP presence in food and human monitoring likewise underscored "the pressing need to establish more robust biomarker research and to develop standardized methodologies, for a better understanding of MPs and NPs fate and associated effects in more realistic scenarios" (Review on "From food-to-human microplastics and nanoplastics exposure and health effects: a review on food, animal and human monitoring data," PubMed PMID 39710246; Semantic Scholar, published 2024-12-01).

**Key summary of reliability issues:**
1. *Contamination during sample handling* can produce false positives; stringent QA/QC protocols are not uniformly applied.
2. *Polymer identification by a single technique is insufficient*; best practice involves combining Raman/FTIR with thermal analysis (Py-GC–MS) and/or electron microscopy, but each method has well-documented limitations in complex matrices.
3. *Size limits matter*: most techniques reliably detect particles >1–5 µm; nanoparticles (<100 nm) require specialized methods that are less widely validated and not yet standardized for clinical use.
4. Without harmonized protocols across labs, "statistical meta-analysis was not appropriate" (Karnaphuli River PRISMA appraisal above).

---

### Bottom Line

Microplastics and nanoplastics have now been **physically detected** in at least blood, carotid artery plaque, human feces, placenta, lung tissue, urinary specimens, and brain samples. An NEJM study found a strong association between MPs/NPs in carotid plaques and cardiovascular events (HR 4.53). Systematic reviews across multiple organ systems conclude that microplastic exposure is **"suspected"** to harm reproductive, digestive, and respiratory health with suggested links to colon and lung cancer, though direct causal evidence in humans remains **limited**. A separate review of animal reproductive-toxicity studies flagged uniformly high risk-of-bias flaws.

**Methodological reliability remains a serious concern.** No single detection technique is sufficient across all matrix types and size ranges; contamination risks are substantial; polymer identification by any one method alone is fragile; and the field urgently lacks standardized, validated analytical protocols for routine clinical interpretation of plastics in human specimens.
